cards.tip: FIX — When customers heard about the voltage switch corrosion and high amperage issues, they were engaged but Juan said 'I just don't want the next tech to come and be like, hey, did they ever bring this up to your attention?' instead of presenting a structured menu of 4+ options with pricing and asking directly 'Which option works for you?'—missing both the options presentation and the close.

FIX — When the customer asked 'How much is that gonna be?' and then said 'let me talk to my wife about it,' you needed to test that buying signal ('Does $1,877 work for your budget?') and then ask directly: 'Perfect—let me get you scheduled for [date], so once you two decide we can get started right away,' instead of leaving it to them to call back.

FIX — When the customer said 'everything's going okay' but both units weren't working, you clarified the problem but missed framing the visit. When you said 'I'm just gonna run my thorough evaluation, figuring out what's going on,' set expectations instead: 'I'll diagnose both systems, show you what I find, and walk you through your options to get this running again. Should take about an hour.' That frame gives customers confidence to approve work and upgrades later.

WIN — When the customer expressed frustration about upstairs cooling issues, you discovered the root cause in the attic and explained it clearly: 'You have a duct that just fell off...it ain't going where it's supposed to be going.' This clarity, backed by photo evidence, transformed the repair from optional to necessary, and the customer immediately approved both the $388 repair and SAM membership.

WIN — Your consequence-driven explanation won the motor start sale. You said 'Your battery's run out of juice... Your compressor is going to start overheating and then it's going to break down your compressor. That's like a four grand change out.' The customer understood that the $474 repair was insurance against a $4,000 compressor failure. When you offered to do it today, the customer closed on himself: 'So let's do the motor start thing.' Lead with the consequence of NOT fixing it, and the customer will ask you to do the work.

WIN — When the customer mentioned the fan running every hour, Stanley immediately identified the root cause, switched it to auto mode, and clearly explained the result; the instant problem-solving earned the customer's confidence and their signature.

FIX — when the customer confirms the problem is active (cycling, warm air at wrong temperature), present the three options (motor device replacement, full unit upgrade, maintenance membership) and pricing right then — waiting until later means the customer's already decided to think about it and you lose the sale to a competitor.

FIX — When customer expressed interest in the air cabinet but said he'd discuss it with his wife, you said 'I'll call Monday'—instead, ask what's really in the way ('cost or her input?'), then lock it in now: 'Details tonight, 6 PM tomorrow with both of you—let's schedule it.' That move—clarifying the objection then committing to a specific time—is where deals close.

FIX — When the customer acknowledged the discolored voltage switch, you said 'I would recommend that in the springtime' instead of asking 'Would you like to go ahead with that replacement today?'—the customer was on-site, knew the issue from your last visit, and was ready; that's where you close.

FIX — When the customer mentioned she does filters quarterly and keeps spares on hand, that's your moment to pitch SAM membership ('we handle all your filter changes, priority scheduling, and typically save you money')—offer the plan instead of just switching them out as a courtesy.

WIN — You showed the dust buildup with a photo, explained how it damages the motor, offered options from $400 cleaning to $3,000 cabinet, and when they chose the $180 filter, you closed immediately with a price quote and signature request—no hesitation, no second-guessing. That's what sealed the deal.

WIN — Your member discount pitch closed this one—when you said 'the $1,351 with member savings from the $1,590,' the customer saw the value and signed; next time, lead with 2-3 price tiers so they're choosing from options, not just hearing one recommendation.

FIX — When your customer said he'd talk to his son, instead of accepting the deferral, ask 'What's his main concern—cost, timeline, or repair versus replace?' and offer 'I can walk you through those now if you want to call him'—stay in the conversation instead of handing off quotes.
WIN — After replacing the motor start device, Tyler reported "Yeah, she's running," which gave the customer immediate proof that the diagnosis was right and justified the $447 cost.

FIX — When the customer asked about cost, you left to write the estimate without first giving a quick verbal options sketch ('soft-start-only at $X or the full package at $Y') and a timeline—instead keep them engaged by saying 'I'll have you those options in about 10 minutes' so you don't lose momentum.

FIX — When the customer signaled the soft start was the right upgrade to protect their new compressor, you should've asked: "Let me get that $1,380 soft start installed for you today" — instead you pivoted to other components and never circled back to close the sale.

WIN — You sealed the membership close by connecting diagnosis to immediate action: after showing the failed capacitor, you asked 'If you guys sign up on the membership today, I can definitely do that summer maintenance... I'll clean up, I'll open it up, test everything on the both units'—giving the customer who'd wanted to join before a concrete reason to stop deferring and act now.

FIX — Jose gave the right recommendation ($1,351 compressor repair) when the customer asked 'which one do you recommend?', but he didn't ask to schedule it; a direct close ('Should we get that scheduled this week?') would have either locked the sale or surfaced the real barrier so Jose could offer financing.

FIX — When the customer expressed budget concerns about filters, you should have pivoted to ask 'What else have you noticed about the system?' and built a tiered good/better/best options menu instead of staying in filter-price negotiation alone.

WIN — You explained the findings clearly ('didn't hit the pipe, looks good'), took photos to document it, and your direct 'How would you like to pay?' got an immediate card tap—straightforward close after solid diagnosis builds trust.

FIX — When you confirmed the pan was level and draining properly, you should have offered the membership agreement to prevent this on all his properties instead of just approving their work and leaving.

FIX — when the customer mentioned the thermostat keeps disconnecting from the app, acknowledge it's a known issue then propose an upgrade: 'I can get you a couple of options for a thermostat that'll connect reliably every time' and ask for the sale—instead you just said you've heard bad things about that app and moved on.

WIN — Adrian confidently communicated 'everything's checking out good' with 'no real concerns,' then directly asked to 'collect your signature' and the customer approved the $39 tune-up without hesitation.
WIN — Finding and fixing both the capacitors and thermostat with clear options and live proof (84° to 60° temp split) won you not just this job, but got them to ditch the other quote.

FIX — When Sean said "Let me think about it" on the surge protection, you reframed the feature instead of asking what was holding him back; since he had just mentioned cash flow pressure with the newborn, offering a payment plan—split the $876 into three $290 monthly payments—would have likely closed that sale.

WIN — When you showed the filter installation and explained 'The UV bulb is still functioning, so that's great,' the customer immediately said 'looks good' and signed without hesitation—professional execution plus clear explanation builds customer confidence to close.
